title: Making a game with AI is surprisingly easy. Making it fun is the hard part. Does this spaceship-building idea have potential?
author: AsnIsCrazyToo
selftext:
Hi everyone!

I'm a solo indie developer working on a game where you build your own spaceship by connecting different parts.

Most of the code is written with AI assistance. I have many years of game development experience, so I focus on designing the systems, making technical decisions, testing, and guiding the AI through implementation.

Honestly, AI has made development much faster than I expected. But I've also realized something: **AI can help me build a game, but it can't tell me whether the game is actually fun.**

Right now, the most enjoyable part is simply assembling a spaceship. It feels a little like playing with LEGO. You connect different weapons, engines, and structural parts, and gradually create something that looks completely your own.

Each component has its own function. Weapons fire from their actual positions, engines provide acceleration, and parts can be destroyed during combat.

But here's where I'm struggling.

I originally wanted to make a roguelite with lots of enemies, frequent upgrades, crazy power growth, and boss fights.

I've experimented with different gameplay directions, including free exploration and traditional scrolling shooter combat. Even small changes completely transform how the game feels.

And sometimes I find that **designing the game is more fun than actually playing it.**

That's a strange and frustrating feeling.

What you're seeing in the video is still a very early prototype, mostly showing the building system and a little combat. There's no polished gameplay loop yet.

Working alone can feel pretty lonely sometimes. I spend a lot of time experimenting, wondering whether I'm heading in the right direction, and occasionally questioning whether anyone would even want to play something like this.

So I'd genuinely love to hear your thoughts:

* Does the idea of building your own spaceship from parts appeal to you?
* Would you prefer this as a roguelite shoot 'em up, or something more focused on exploration and building?
* Does the assembly mechanic itself look satisfying, or does it need something more?

I'm not promoting a finished game or asking anyone to wishlist it. I'm just trying to find out whether this idea has potential.

Any honest feedback, criticism, or encouragement would mean a lot.

Thanks for watching!

comments.author: sseses
comments.body:
I think it has promise. The shooting looks fun at least :) I do like designing space ships...

I can relate to how you said designing games these days ends up being more fun than the actual playing itself. Its definitely a strange feeling.

As a game designer though doesn't a game become 'unfun' after enough playtesting -- don't you get burnt out? Especially in the pre ai era! I remember how long Diablo 3 took to come out -- Blizzard was practically locking them in when they went past deadline. I would have been sick of that game after 3 years of grinding (actually I guess it was 10+ years of grinding! holy shit: https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1x28k0v/making\_a\_game\_with\_ai\_is\_surprisingly\_easy\_making/)

I feel like its hard to figure out what that last 5 percent of the game should be -- and I've built out a number of prototypes, the foundation and architecture these days is the easy part.

That one signature game dynamic? Still in the domain of creativity, and elusive as ever 🥸

Have you tried harassing your friends and asking for playtests and brutal feedback? I'm starting to go thru that process on some of my projects :)

replies.body: Great advice! Your background music is very attractive. How can you make it? I need music for my game.

replies.author: DebtResponsible7868
replies.body:
Have the AI download 100 sound effects of the type you want, with licenses that allow reuse.
Have it write a description of each sound in your language (15 characters max).
Have it build an app that plays them sequentially and lets you select sounds by clicking.
Finally, have it perform an adversarial review to check for any copyright or licensing issues.

This is how I'm doing it right now using Claude, but I feel like there must be a better way. GL HF!

replies.author: AsnIsCrazyToo
replies.body: Thanks for sharing! That's a really clever workflow. I especially like the idea of using AI to build a tool for quickly previewing and selecting sounds, rather than having AI make the final choice. I'll definitely give this a try!
